title: The four properties of consumer preferences
summary: Completeness, more is better, diminishing marginal rate of substitution (with the 50, 16.67, 8.33 numbers) and transitivity.

chunks.heading: Completeness
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide lists four properties of consumer preference ordering: **completeness**, **more is better**, **diminishing marginal rate of substitution** and **transitivity**.

**Completeness:** the consumer can express a preference (or indifference) between **all possible bundles**. "I don't know" is **not** an option.

Example: if the only bundles are A, B and C, the consumer is **indifferent between A and C** (same indifference curve), **prefers B to A** and **prefers B to C**.

key_terms.meaning: The consumer can express preferences or indifference between all possible bundles.

chunks.exam_line: Completeness: a consumer can rank every pair of bundles; 'I don't know' is not an option.

chunks.heading: More is better
chunks.explanation_md:
**More is better:** bundles with **at least as much of every good and more of some good** are preferred.

On the graph, A is at X = 1, Y = 100; B is at X = 3, Y = 100; C is at X = 3, Y = 33.33.

- **B is preferred to A**: same amount of Y, **strictly more X**.
- **B is preferred to C**: same amount of X, **strictly more Y**.
- Generally, all bundles on **IC III** are preferred to those on IC II or IC I, and all on **IC II** are preferred to IC I. Higher curves mean more satisfaction.

key_terms.meaning: Bundles with at least as much of every good and more of some good are preferred.

chunks.exam_line: More is better: B beats A (more X, same Y) and beats C (more Y, same X). Higher indifference curves are preferred.

check_questions.answer: Same Y and strictly more X

chunks.heading: Diminishing marginal rate of substitution
chunks.explanation_md:
**Diminishing marginal rate of substitution:** the amount of Y the consumer is willing to give up to stay equally satisfied **decreases as more X is acquired**.

The slide's bundles on IC I: A at X = 1, Y = 100; B at X = 2, Y = 50; C at X = 3, Y = 33.33; D at X = 4, Y = 25.

| Move | Y given up for one more X |
|---|---|
| A to B | 50 units |
| B to C | 16.67 units |
| C to D | only 8.33 units |

The more X you have, the less Y you will give up for one more X. That is why indifference curves are **bowed in toward the origin**.

key_terms.meaning: The amount of Y given up to keep the same satisfaction falls as more X is acquired.

chunks.exam_line: marginal rate of substitution diminishes: A to B gives up 50 of Y, B to C 16.67, C to D only 8.33, for one extra unit of X each time.

chunks.heading: Transitivity
chunks.explanation_md:
**Transitivity:** for three bundles A, B and C, if the consumer prefers C to B and B to A, then the consumer prefers **C to A**.

Transitive preferences, together with more-is-better, imply that:

- **indifference curves will not intersect**;
- the consumer will **not get caught in a perpetual cycle of indecision**.

key_terms.meaning: If C is preferred to B and B to A, then C is preferred to A.

chunks.exam_line: Transitivity: C over B and B over A means C over A. With more is better it means indifference curves do not cross.

questions.stem: Name and briefly explain the four properties of consumer preference ordering.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Completeness**: the consumer can express a preference or indifference between all possible bundles.
2. **More is better**: bundles with at least as much of every good and more of some good are preferred.
3. **Diminishing marginal rate of substitution**: the amount of Y given up for another X falls as more X is acquired.
4. **Transitivity**: if C is preferred to B and B to A, then C is preferred to A.

questions.model_answer_md:
A is at X = 1, Y = 100; B is at X = 3, Y = 100; C is at X = 3, Y = 33.33.

- **B over A**: same Y and strictly more X.
- **B over C**: same X and strictly more Y.

Generally, bundles on a higher indifference curve (III over II over I) are preferred.

questions.stem: Using the slide's bundles A (X = 1, Y = 100), B (X = 2, Y = 50), C (X = 3, Y = 33.33) and D (X = 4, Y = 25), calculate how much Y the consumer gives up for each extra unit of X and comment.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Move | Y given up |
|---|---|
| A to B | 100 - 50 = 50 |
| B to C | 50 - 33.33 = 16.67 |
| C to D | 33.33 - 25 = 8.33 |

The amount of Y given up falls as more X is acquired: this is the **diminishing marginal rate of substitution**.

questions.stem: State transitivity and explain what it implies for indifference curves.
questions.model_answer_md:
For three bundles A, B and C, transitivity says that if C is preferred to B and B is preferred to A, then **C is preferred to A**.

With more-is-better it implies indifference curves **will not intersect** and the consumer will **not get caught in a perpetual cycle of indecision**.

questions.stem: Explain the diminishing marginal rate of substitution using the numerical example on the slides.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** The marginal rate of substitution is the rate at which a consumer swaps one good for another and keeps the same satisfaction. It diminishes as more X is acquired.

**Example.** On indifference curve I the consumer holds A (X = 1, Y = 100), B (X = 2, Y = 50), C (X = 3, Y = 33.33) and D (X = 4, Y = 25).
- A to B: give up 50 units of Y for one extra X.
- B to C: give up 16.67.
- C to D: give up only 8.33.

**Meaning.** The more X the consumer has, the less Y is willing to be sacrificed for yet another X.

**Conclusion.** This is why indifference curves bend toward the origin.

rubric.point: Y given up falls as X rises

questions.stem: Discuss the properties of completeness, more is better and transitivity and show how each is illustrated on the slides.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** Three properties make consumer preferences consistent.

**Completeness.** The consumer can express preference or indifference between all bundles; 'I don't know' is not an option. With A, B and C, the consumer is indifferent between A and C and prefers B to both.

**More is better.** Bundle B is preferred to A (same Y, more X) and to C (same X, more Y); bundles on IC III beat IC II and IC I.

**Transitivity.** If C is preferred to B and B to A, then C is preferred to A. This means curves do not intersect.

**Conclusion.** Together these give well-behaved indifference curves.
